name: Omar Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the season. Right now, November, it's drilling the last of the winter wheat and checking the feedlot, we've got about four hundred head of beef cattle on top of the arable. I'm the crop and machinery lead at Harlow Farms, which is a family company, three brothers own it, about 600 hectares of wheat, canola and grass. I run two drivers and a seasonal crew in summer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting a field right, a straight drill line, an even crop coming through in spring, you can see your work from the road. What wears me out is the pay versus the hours. My partner Lina is a nurse at the district hospital, and between her nights and my harvest weeks we sometimes don't see each other for days, and we still end most months with almost nothing left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then. At work I'd joke with the brothers that they can stop reading tech magazines over lunch. Online I'd probably say the real problems were never the robots, they were wages and land prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means nothing changes, which isn't the same as fine. I'd still be on the lower end of pay for a guy with a degree, with a few weeks of money in the bank. The things that would help me were never about AI anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, mostly. I use a chatbot now and then to check a spray label or translate a manual for the new drill, and I'd keep doing that. I'd keep pushing the brothers on a pay review in January, and keep paying into the farmworkers' union, which I joined last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit of relief, a bit of 'so what was all the noise for'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the real problems were wages and land prices. Which one hits you hardest right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land, long term. I'll never own a field on what I earn, and with prices where they are, nobody my age will. I can grow a perfect crop on someone else's ground for forty years and retire with a nice photo of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if your pay review in January came back with nothing, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look around, but there's not much. There are maybe three farms within an hour that hire someone at my level, and they all pay about the same. So I'd probably grumble and stay, honestly.

S0.say: I'd say the real problems were never robots, they were wages and land prices. At work I'd joke that the owners can stop reading tech magazines over lunch.
S0.think: It means nothing changes, which isn't the same as fine. I'd still be underpaid for my degree, with a few weeks of money in the bank.
S0.do: Keeps using a chatbot now and then for spray labels and machine manuals. Pushes the owners for a pay review in January and keeps paying into the farmworkers' union.
S0.feel: Calm, with some relief and some irritation at all the noise.
S0.quote: I can grow a perfect crop on someone else's ground for forty years and retire with a nice photo of it.
S0.fieldNote: He turns the AI question straight into a question about land ownership. The 'perfect crop on someone else's ground' line is the heart of his frustration. He's realistic that with few local jobs he'd likely stay even if the pay review fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Okay, next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when you need a strong union and a government that pays for retraining. Change itself is fine. I'd say that at the pub and I'd share stuff online about workers getting a share of what the machines save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm one of the lucky ones, kind of. I already run the machines, so if the drills and sprayers start driving themselves, someone still has to set them up and fix them. But my two drivers, Raj and Tom, I'm not so sure about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till the first farms round here have the self-steering kit working for a season, then I'd ask the brothers to send me on the dealer's course. I'd want to be the guy who knows it before they hire someone from outside. I'd also try to put a hundred a month aside, though with Lina's car loan that's hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, not scared. Like a weather forecast for rain at harvest, you plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure about Raj and Tom. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight, learn the kit or push for the union deal, because I can't protect your hours. Tom's twenty-two and he'd pick it up. Raj has been driving tractors longer than I've been alive, and I'd have to be the one telling him the tractor drives itself now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait until other farms have it working. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the brothers buy shiny things before. They bought a soil scanner three years ago that sits in the shed because the subscription went up. I'd rather let someone else pay for the mistakes.

S1.say: I'd say this is when you need a strong union and government-paid retraining. I'd share stuff online about workers getting a share of what the machines save.
S1.think: I think I'm one of the lucky ones, because I already run the machines and someone has to set them up. My two drivers are the ones I'd worry about.
S1.do: Waits until local farms have used self-steering kit for a season, then asks the owners to send him on the dealer's course. Tries to save a hundred a month despite his partner's car loan.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not scared, like a forecast for rain at harvest that you plan around.
S1.quote: Raj has been driving tractors longer than I've been alive, and I'd have to be the one telling him the tractor drives itself now.
S1.fieldNote: He's steady to the core: open to the new kit, but only after someone else proves it. His sense of safety rests on his machinery role, and his worry goes to the drivers he manages. The soil scanner story shows why he distrusts being first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now three bigger pictures. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that was allowed to happen, and that the companies who built it should pay for every job it takes. I'd be posting about a tax on robots and a basic income. I'd say it loudly, because if it's two years, there's no time to be polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my 'I run the machines' safety net goes. If the AI can fix and set up the kit too, then the brothers need one person to watch a screen, and maybe it's one of the brothers. With a few weeks of savings, that's a scary place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut everything, Lina and I would sell her car and share mine. I'd go to every union meeting and probably to a protest in the capital. Once it arrived, I'd hope Lina's nursing job holds a bit longer, and I'd lean on that and whatever the government puts in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the moment you hear the combine make a noise it's never made before, halfway down a field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very little time. Is there anything that short warning lets you do at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for me. Two years is one and a half harvests. You can't save for a new life in a year and a half on farm wages, you can just about save for a new tyre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on Lina's job. How would that conversation go between you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awkward, honestly. I was always the one saying we'd buy a place in the country one day. She'd say it's fine, we're a team, and she'd mean it, but I'd hate it, and I know that's my problem, not hers.

S2.say: I'd say this disaster was allowed to happen and the companies who built it should pay for every job it takes. I'd push for a robot tax and a basic income, loudly.
S2.think: My safety net of running the machines goes, because the AI can set them up too. With a few weeks of savings that's a scary place to be.
S2.do: Cuts spending straight away and sells his partner's car so they share one. Goes to union meetings and a protest in the capital, then leans on his partner's nursing income and public support once AGI arrives.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like hearing the combine make a new noise halfway down a field.
S2.quote: You can't save for a new life in a year and a half on farm wages, you can just about save for a new tyre.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline removes the thing that made him feel safe in steady change. He's honest about his pride: being supported by his partner is hard for him, and he owns it as his problem. Blame goes to the companies building the technology and to policy, not to his employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, get the laws in place and get the training paid for. I'd say farmers and farm workers need to be in the room, not just tech people. I'd probably be the one at the union meeting with a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years probably buys me three or four good years on the machinery side. People will still need a person on site to set things up while it's spreading. But after that, I'm not sure, and I don't want to kid myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the dealer course in the first year, this time not waiting. I'd also start a basic online course in electrics, in the evenings, because whatever comes, things need wiring. And we'd save, properly, maybe two hundred a month once Lina's car is paid off next autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. There's a to-do list in my head already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said this time you wouldn't wait. What's changed from the steady picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the steady one, waiting costs nothing. Here, waiting a year costs you a fifth of your time. Being careful is a luxury when the clock's only got five years on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're planning electrics. Would you stay on the farm, or go elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to stay round here, but electricians go where the work is. Lina could get a nursing job almost anywhere, which helps. If we had to move to the city for a few years, we would.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so get the laws in place and get training paid for. Farmers and farm workers need to be in the room, not just tech people.
S3.think: Five years probably buys me three or four good years on the machinery side. After that I don't know, and I don't want to kid myself.
S3.do: Takes the dealer's machinery course in the first year instead of waiting, and starts an evening course in electrics. Saves around two hundred a month once his partner's car is paid off next autumn.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a to-do list already forming.
S3.quote: Being careful is a luxury when the clock's only got five years on it.
S3.fieldNote: The middle timeline flips his usual caution: he names that waiting costs too much here. He's practical about moving to the city if electrical work is there. His progressive politics stay steady, but his personal plan becomes much more active.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so if we mess it up, that's on us. I'd want a plan where the gains from machines go into land trusts, public training, maybe shorter hours for everyone. I'd say that at the pub and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to switch careers properly. I might even be one of the people installing the machines that replace farms like Harlow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the dealer course, then get a full electrician's qualification over three or four years, part-time, while still working at Harlow. I'd join the union's working group on automation if they set one up. Lina and I would probably hold off on buying a house until it's clearer where work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly okay. Almost interested, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on a house. Is that a big change for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. We've been looking at an old cottage near Lina's parents. I'd rather rent for five more years than buy a house in a village that might not have a single farm job left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, you sound almost interested. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years I get to choose. With two, it just happens to me. I'm fine with change if I can see it coming and get ready for it, I just hate being rushed.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so if we mess it up it's on us. The gains from machines should go into land trusts, public training and shorter hours.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable, and at thirty-seven I'm young enough to switch careers properly. I might end up installing the machines myself.
S4.do: Takes the dealer's course, then works towards a full electrician's qualification part-time over three or four years while staying at the farm. Joins any union working group on automation and holds off on buying a house with his partner.
S4.feel: Uneasy at the back of his mind, but mostly okay and even a bit interested.
S4.quote: I'd rather rent for five more years than buy a house in a village that might not have a single farm job left.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he moves from fear to something close to curiosity, because he gets to choose. Delaying the cottage purchase is a real cost he names plainly. His line about hating being rushed sums up how timing drives his whole reaction.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to do the things I know how to do, which is plan and learn once I've seen something work. What would help is paid retraining that you can do while still on a wage, and some kind of income guarantee for the gap. The machines will be fine, it's the year between jobs that'll break people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the farms afterwards. If it's all robots, then whoever owns the land and the robots owns the food. That should worry people a lot more than it does.

headlineQuote: The machines will be fine, it's the year between jobs that'll break people.
portrait: Omar Tanaka is a 27-year-old crop and machinery lead on a 600-hectare family company farm, with a degree, low pay and only a few weeks of savings, living with his partner Lina, a nurse. He leans left, belongs to the farmworkers' union and uses AI tools now and then, but he likes to see new kit proven before he backs it. He's calm if AI is hype and only uneasy in steady change, because he already runs the machines. Fast AGI alarms him, and he'd lean on Lina's income, which hurts his pride. With five or ten years he becomes much more active, training as an electrician and putting off buying a house.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's no time to plan and learn once he's seen something work.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining he can do while still earning, and an income guarantee to get through the gap between jobs.
